power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective: By what mechanisms does parental monitoring affect youth adjustment?
This paper aimed to review every published study that has tested a statistical mediator of monitoring→adjustment.

Method: We searched for studies that (a) enrolled elementary-, middle-, and/or high-school aged youth, (b) measured parental monitoring as parent action (vs., e.g., knowledge), and (c) tested a statistical mediation model linking monitoring to any form of youth adjustment.
Results: 39 papers have tested a mediator of the link from monitoring → adjustment.
Most papers used cross-sectional data only (26 of 39) on typically developing samples (33 of 39).
All papers were non-experimental.
Only 1 of 39 papers made a substantial effort to rule out potential confounding -most adjusted for just a few measured covariates.
Across the 39 papers, 79 out of 173 tests of mediation were statistically significant (46%).
Of the significant tests, 59 indicated beneficial effects of monitoring, and 20 indicated detrimental effects of monitoring.
There was at least one statistically significant test for 42 distinct pairs of mediator and outcome, but only 6 mediational chains had been replicated in more than one paper.
Effect sizes for single mediators were typically small (median standardized ab = -0.02) and suggested multiple mediators would be needed to explain the total effect (median percent mediated = 24%).
Of relevance to Stattin and Kerr's (2000) classic argument, we found only 1 paper testing whether youth disclosure mediates the link between monitoring and adjustment.
text.formatted: Of relevance to <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stattin and Kerr's (2000)</ref> classic argument, we found only 1 paper testing whether youth disclosure mediates the link between monitoring and adjustment.

text.text: Conclusion: There are now many published tests of the mediators linking parental monitoring to youth adjustment.
However, few have been replicated, and fewer still have been rigorous.
As a result, the extant evidence can be reconciled with many (if not all) major theories about how parental monitoring works.

In their classic papers (Stattin & Kerr, 2000; Kerr & Stattin, 2000), Stattin and Kerr conceptualize youth disclosure as a competitor to parental monitoring -another independent variable that competes to explain adjustment (Figure 1, Model A).
text.formatted: In their classic papers (Stattin & Kerr, 2000; Kerr & Stattin, 2000), Stattin and Kerr conceptualize youth disclosure as a competitor to parental monitoring -another independent variable that competes to explain adjustment (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, <ref type="figure">Model A</ref>).

text.text: But youth disclosure could also be a mediator for parental monitoring -the parent asks for information (X), then the teen discloses information (M), and in turn we see improved adjustment (Y) (Figure 1, Model B).
text.formatted: But youth disclosure could also be a mediator for parental monitoring -the parent asks for information (X), then the teen discloses information (M), and in turn we see improved adjustment (Y) (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, Model B).

text.text: This is a perfectly natural mediation chain to hypothesize.

Unfortunately, the competitor vs. mediator possibilities cannot be empirically distinguished when monitoring and disclosure are measured at the same timepoint, as they were in Stattin and Kerr's landmark papers.
The competitor and mediator models will give identical model fit, standardized coefficients, and p-values (MacKinnon et al., 2000).
text.formatted: The competitor and mediator models will give identical model fit, standardized coefficients, and p-values <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(MacKinnon et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, an alternative interpretation of Stattin and Kerr's classic finding is not that disclosure is a competitor or replacement for monitoring, as they argue, but simply a mediating mechanism by which monitoring affects adjustment.
Stattin and Kerr (2000a, 2000b)  did not acknowledge this possibility; in a later paper, Kerr, Stattin, and Burk (2010) discussed it but did not test it directly.
2 Pending tests of mediation in longitudinal data, what to make of Stattin and Kerr's classic finding remains unclear.
This paper aimed to review every published study that has tested a statistical mediator of the link between monitoring and adjustment -including those that have tested youth disclosure in particular.
We aimed to synthesize and evaluate the evidence for each putative mediator, both in isolation and in comparison.
The goal was to inform core questions first raised by Stattin and Kerr (2000) -whether and how monitoring works, and the role of disclosure within that picture.
text.formatted: The goal was to inform core questions first raised by <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stattin and Kerr (2000)</ref> -whether and how monitoring works, and the role of disclosure within that picture.

text.text: We define "parental monitoring" as the set of behaviors parents perform with the goal of gaining information about their teenager's activities and life (Pelham et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We define "parental monitoring" as the set of behaviors parents perform with the goal of gaining information about their teenager's activities and life <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Pelham et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, this review focuses exclusively on monitoring as parent action -a superset of the constructs Stattin shook up the field with a dramatic empirical claim.
First, they showed that the burgeoning literature ostensibly linking "parental monitoring" to youth adjustment had in fact been linking parental knowledge to youth adjustment.
The items on scales labeled "parental monitoring" mostly asked about what parents knew, not what parents did.
Second, Stattin and Kerr fixed the measurement issue by creating new scales to carefully measure parental monitoring as a parent behavior.

After fixing the measurement issue, they found that the cross-sectional association between parental monitoring and youth adjustment (specifically, normbreaking) went from (a) positive and statistically significant to (b) near zero and statistically nonsignificant when one adjusted for concomitant youth disclosure.
This finding sparked a major shift in thinking about parental monitoring and has guided the past 25 years of research on an important topic.
Stattin and Kerr started a conversation about whether and how parental monitoring actually works.
Yet it is difficult to test whether something works until you specify the mechanisms by which that something should produce its effects.
The mechanistic theory guides what should be measured, when, and tells you what counts as evidence for or against efficacy.
Consider the analogy of testing a new medication for depression.
Does it work via active concentration in the bloodstream?
If so, a good way to test efficacy would be to administer the medication once in the lab and then measure momentary depressive symptoms after administration.

But a bad way to test efficacy would be to prescribe the pill to be taken at home every day for 15 days, then measure depression in a lab visit 6 months later -you'd find no differences, because the medication would no longer be in the bloodstream.
Now suppose the medication works via long-term accumulation in fat cells and becomes effective only once a certain concentration is reached.
If so, the lab administration study would (incorrectly) yield null results and the at-home follow-up study would (correctly) yield positive results.
So, when it comes to testing whether parental monitoring works, what are the hypothesized mechanisms?
Unfortunately, the field has not reached a consensus (Pelham et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Unfortunately, the field has not reached a consensus <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pelham et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Most articles linking monitoring to youth adjustment do not articulate any mechanistic theory, perhaps because the link seems self-explanatory, and those articles that do articulate a mechanism often propose conflicting ones.

For example, some authors emphasize disciplinary practices (e.g., Hayes et al., 2003), others peer affiliation (e.g., Patterson & Dishion, 1985), others the internalization of parent values (e.g., Omer et al., 2016), and others still the development of self-control (e.g., Unnever & Cornell, 2003).
text.formatted: For example, some authors emphasize disciplinary practices (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hayes et al., 2003)</ref>, others peer affiliation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Patterson & Dishion, 1985)</ref>, others the internalization of parent values (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Omer et al., 2016)</ref>, and others still the development of self-control (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Unnever & Cornell, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: When theories disagree to this extent, a logical next step is to evaluate them with empirical evidence -to collect and compare studies that have tested mediating mechanisms.

Interestingly, Stattin and Kerr did not propose a mechanism that links parental monitoring to teen adjustment. 1 Rather they proposed there was no effect to explain, because their regression analysis showed that youth disclosure, not monitoring, is what causes differences in youth adjustment (or parental knowledge).

text.text: One problem with that reasoning is the one described above: until you've articulated how something is supposed to work, it is difficult to test whether it works.
But there is an even deeper methodological problem, demonstrated in Figure 1. and Kerr labeled "solicitation" and "control" in their landmark papers.

text.text: We define "parental knowledge" as information the parent has about the teen's activities and life.
We define "youth disclosure" as the youth intentionally communicating true information about their activities or life to their parent.

We stick to these definitions throughout this article. Stattin and Kerr (2000) and Stattin et al. (2010) documented that in many articles on the topic of parental monitoring, the labels given to the measures do not match the item content -scales measuring knowledge, a mix of knowledge and monitoring, or even a mix of knowledge, monitoring, and disclosure, all labeled "parental monitoring."

(2010)</ref> documented that in many articles on the topic of parental monitoring, the labels given to the measures do not match the item content -scales measuring knowledge, a mix of knowledge and monitoring, or even a mix of knowledge, monitoring, and disclosure, all labeled "parental monitoring."

text.text: For this reason, we always checked the item content of the "monitoring" measure in the studies we wished to include -going by what was actually measured, rather than the labels the authors gave the measure.
We searched for papers examining mediators of the association between parental monitoring and youth adjustment.
We searched PubMed, Google Scholar, ProQuest, and the University of California, San Diego library databases.
The first and third authors performed the searches between May 2025 and April 2026.

We searched for every pairwise combination of the following search terms: ("parental monitoring" OR "parental solicitation" OR "parental control" OR "parental behavioral control" OR "parental supervision") + ("mediator" OR "mechanism" OR "mediation" OR "path analysis" OR "structural equation model" OR "mediating mechanism").

We also reviewed the reference lists in review papers on the topic of monitoring (Dishion & McMahon, 1998; Crouter et al., 2002; Stattin et al., 2010; Racz & McMahon, 2011; Anderson & Branstetter, 2012; Tilton-Weaver & Marshall, 2024; Pelham et al., 2024; Pelham et al., 2025; Aks et al., 2025) and of every article that we determined met the inclusion/exclusion criteria.
text.formatted: We also reviewed the reference lists in review papers on the topic of monitoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dishion & McMahon, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Crouter et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Stattin et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Racz & McMahon, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Anderson & Branstetter, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Tilton-Weaver & Marshall, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Pelham et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pelham et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Aks et al., 2025)</ref> and of every article that we determined met the inclusion/exclusion criteria.

text.text: Finally, we emailed the corresponding author of every included paper and several known experts in the field of parental monitoring to inquire whether they knew of any relevant articles we had missed.

Papers were considered for inclusion if they met four criteria: (a) reported on parental monitoring in a sample of elementary-, middle-, and/or high-school aged youth, (b) measured parental monitoring per the definition above, (c) measured any form of youth adjustment (e.g., behavioral, psychiatric, academic), and (d) statistically tested whether the association between monitoring and adjustment was mediated by a third variable.
Many papers measured parental monitoring using a rating scale that included some items that met our definition and some items that did not (e.g., Jin et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Many papers measured parental monitoring using a rating scale that included some items that met our definition and some items that did not (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jin et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In such cases, we included the study as long as ≥70% of the items on the measure met our definition of parental monitoring.
If there was doubt about whether the measure qualified, reviewers searched for the exact item content and contacted the author for the complete list of items if necessary.
We included papers published in any year, whether or not they had been peer-reviewed.
Every paper identified for inclusion was checked by a second reviewer to confirm eligibility.
Disagreements were discussed among both reviewers and the senior author to reach a decision.
The first and third authors completed the data extraction.
After one of these authors had extracted the data, the other author checked each value.
Any discrepancies were resolved via discussion with the senior author.

For each paper, we extracted the following information: (a) the number of participants; (b) the sociodemographic composition; (c) the study design, (d) the temporal order in which X, M, and Y were measured; and (e) the specific measures used for X, M, and Y.
We categorized monitoring measures (X) using a typology we outlined in a prior paper (Pelham et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We categorized monitoring measures (X) using a typology we outlined in a prior paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Pelham et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Type 1 monitoring refers to asking a person for information (often called "solicitation").
Type 2 monitoring refers to setting or enforcing rules to gather information (often called "control").
Type 3 monitoring refers to using objective records to gather information (e.g., checking the teen's grades in an online portal).
Type 4 monitoring refers to observing the youth to gather information (e.g., watching what the teen is doing while friends are over).
For each paper, we examined the monitoring scale's item content and determined which type(s) of monitoring were being measured.
For each test of mediation, we extracted the following information: (a) the a path, (b) the b path, (c) the c' path, and (d) the covariates included in each regression.
For each path, we extracted the coefficient, standard error, p-value, and 95% confidence interval.

We also extracted the estimates of the standardized indirect effect (ab), the percent mediated (ab / c), the total effect (c), and the zero-order correlation between monitoring and youth adjustment (r xy ).
If these values were not reported, we calculated them ourselves where possible (see supplement for details).
The scope and form of the located evidence did not permit meta-analysis.
Instead, we qualitatively evaluated patterns of effect size and statistical significance, both as a whole and by characteristics of the sample/design.
We also evaluated methodological features (e.g., number and choice of covariates) that might affect the rigor of the underlying test.
Tests of sequential or moderated mediation were tabulated separately and are reported after the main results, in their own sections.
Some youth adjustment outcomes were things one would want to prevent (e.g., delinquency) and others were things one would want to encourage (e.g., grade point average).
As a result, the sign of the monitoring ↔ outcome association must be interpreted with care.

To simplify presentation, we rescaled every effect size before tabulation so that a negative value indicates a beneficial effect of parental monitoring (e.g., greater monitoring → lower delinquency) and a positive value indicates a detrimental effect of parental monitoring (e.g., greater monitoring → greater delinquency).
Our initial searches yielded 164 papers that might meet inclusion/exclusion criteria.

Further review excluded all but 39 of these papers. 67 papers were excluded because, while the paper claimed to measure parental monitoring, the measure did not match the definition of parental monitoring given above (e.g., it actually measured parental knowledge, as in Patterson & Dishion, 1985). 22 papers were excluded because the measure of monitoring was too contaminated with items assessing other constructs (e.g., Ellis et al., 2007).

Across the 39 included articles, there were 173 unique tests of mediation.

Only 1 out of 4 tests completed on a special education sample were statistically significant -this test was beneficial.
Only 1 test of mediation was completed on a sample of youth with a physical health condition (diabetes) -this test was statistically significant and the indirect effect was beneficial.
Findings by youth age.
Samples included youth in late childhood (ages 8-10) (55 tests), early adolescence (ages 11-13) (127 tests), middle adolescence (ages 14-16) (144 tests), and late adolescence (ages 17-18) (98 tests).
Most papers sampled across multiple age groups, so comparing results based on age was not possible.
Findings in cross-sectional vs. longitudinal studies. 59 out of 119 tests of mediation performed in cross-sectional data yielded statistically significant results (50%).

Of the 59 statistically significant tests in cross-sectional data, the indirect effect of monitoring was beneficial in 43 tests and detrimental in 16 tests (73% beneficial). 20 out of 54 tests of mediation performed in longitudinal data were statistically significant (37%).
Of the 20 statistically significant tests in longitudinal data, the indirect effect was beneficial in 16 tests and detrimental in 4 tests (80% beneficial).
The direct effect of monitoring → adjustment was statistically significant (p<.05) in 43 of the 173 tests (25%).

text.text: The direct effect was beneficial in 30 significant tests and detrimental in 13 significant tests.
The standardized direct effect was reported for 62 of the 173 tests (36%).
The standardized direct effect ranged from -0.65 to 0.20, with a median value of 0.07 (mean = 0.02).
The total effect of monitoring → adjustment was reported for only 24 out of 173 tests.
Of the 18 total effects that reported statistical significance, 14 were significant (78%). 12 significant tests were beneficial and 2 significant tests were detrimental.
The standardized total effect was reported for only 9 of the 173 tests (5%).
The standardized total effect ranged from -0.18 to 0.09, with a median of 0.004 (mean = -0.04).
As a proxy for the total effect, we found a zero-order correlation between monitoring and adjustment for 80 of 173 tests. 56 of 80 zero-order correlations were statistically significant (70%).
Of the significant correlations, 52 were beneficial and 4 were detrimental.
The median zero-order correlation between monitoring and adjustment was -0.13 (range = [-0.33, 0.18]).

Tests of sequential mediation. 6 of 39 articles tested sequential mediation (Fletcher et al., 2004; Kiesner et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Saputra et al., 2025).

text.text: Every sequential chain included 2 mediators. 8 out of 17 tests of sequential mediation were statistically significant (47%), and the sequential indirect effect was beneficial in all 8 significant tests.
There was no obvious pattern distinguishing the papers that decided to test sequential mediation vs. test single mediation.
Tests of moderated mediation. 6 of the 39 articles tested moderated mediation.
The most commonly tested moderator was adolescent gender, tested in 4 articles.

Neither Zhao et al. (2020) nor Fung and Liu (2026) found significant moderation by gender when testing the indirect effect of monitoring on delinquency and aggression. text.text: We found 39 such studies with a combined N of 48,709.
Despite a large number of tests of mediation (k = 173), the studies had serious methodological limitations and the resulting body of evidence remains equivocal.
Ultimately, the pattern of findings shown in Table 2 can be reconciled with many (if not all) major theories about how parental monitoring works.

text.text: Discussion years after
text.formatted: <head>Discussion</head> <head n="25">years after</head>

text.text: The most striking finding of this review is that the field does not have rigorous, replicated evidence for any particular mediating mechanism and target outcome.

There are over 1,640 articles in PubMed that mention parental monitoring in the title or abstract. 3 Yet we found only 39 articles that have tested a mediator of the effect of parental monitoring on youth adjustment, 2 of which were unpublished theses.
text.formatted: There are over 1,640 articles in PubMed that mention parental monitoring in the title or abstract. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_4">3</ref> Yet we found only 39 articles that have tested a mediator of the effect of parental monitoring on youth adjustment, 2 of which were unpublished theses.

text.text: Only 9 articles have tested mediation in a longitudinal sample and 0 articles have tested mediation in a clinical sample.
Although 71 different combinations of mediator and outcome have been tested, only 6 have been replicated in more than one paper.
Figure 2 tentatively summarizes the state of the evidence, depicting every mediational chain that has been statistically significant in at least 2 papers.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref> tentatively summarizes the state of the evidence, depicting every mediational chain that has been statistically significant in at least 2 papers.

text.text: Parental knowledge was the most commonly tested mediator, comprising 23 of the 173 tests (coming from 6 papers).
Yet even for parental knowledge, the evidence was equivocal.
Only 10 of the 23 tests were statistically significant; only 2 of the 23 ensured X < M < Y, both coming from the same paper, and both adjusting for just 4 measured covariates.
text.formatted: Only 10 of the 23 tests were statistically significant; only 2 of the 23 ensured X < M < Y, both coming from the same paper, and both adjusting for just 4 measured covariates.

text.text: Some widely assumed channels have never been tested.

For example, no study has tested whether parental monitoring increases the probability of being punished for a given rule-breaking behavior and in turn decreases the rate of that behavior (operant conditioning).
Other widely assumed channels have been tested repeatedly, but with results that do not offer clear support for them.

For example, there were 10 tests of peer affiliation as the mediator: 5 tests that were not statistically significant, 3 tests showing significant beneficial effects via increased prosocial peers, and 2 tests showing a significant detrimental effect via increased deviant peers.
This package of results is hardly convincing evidence for peer affiliation as a mediator.
The bulk of the evidence pertained to mediators of externalizing outcomes such as delinquency, substance use, and aggression (~70% of all tests).
There were very few tests of mediation with outcomes like internalizing problems, academic functioning, victimization, or sleep.
The mediating mechanisms might be quite different when the target outcome is not a rule-breaking behavior that parents prohibit, but the literature to date cannot probe this possibility.
The evidence we did find suffered from two major limitations on rigor.

The first is the lack of clear temporal precedence. 69% of tests were in cross-sectional data, and only 5 of 39 papers (13%) used three waves of data to ensure X preceded M and M preceded Y. Tests of mediation in cross-sectional data can be highly misleading (Maxwell & Cole, 2007) and cannot rule out reverse causality -that Y or M causes X, or M causes X. Reverse causality is quite plausible in the context of the variables of interest here -monitoring, adjustment, and the putative mediating mechanisms (e.g., peers, parent-youth relationships) -making the heavy reliance on cross-sectional associations more concerning.

Tests of mediation in cross-sectional data can be highly misleading <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Maxwell & Cole, 2007)</ref> and cannot rule out reverse causality -that Y or M causes X, or M causes X. Reverse causality is quite plausible in the context of the variables of interest here -monitoring, adjustment, and the putative mediating mechanisms (e.g., peers, parent-youth relationships) -making the heavy reliance on cross-sectional associations more concerning.

text.text: The second major limitation on rigor is that all 39 studies were non-experimental (i.e., uncontrolled).
Non-experimental tests of mediation assume there is no unmeasured confounding of three different associations: X→M, M→Y, and X→Y (Valente et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Non-experimental tests of mediation assume there is no unmeasured confounding of three different associations: X→M, M→Y, and X→Y <ref type="bibr">(Valente et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: That is not a plausible assumption in the case of monitoring; prior work has confirmed families with different levels of monitoring also differ on dozens of characteristics that could explain differences in mediators or outcomes (Davis et al., 2024).
text.formatted: That is not a plausible assumption in the case of monitoring; prior work has confirmed families with different levels of monitoring also differ on dozens of characteristics that could explain differences in mediators or outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Davis et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The 39 included studies tended to control for just a few covariates -most commonly sociodemographic characteristics, rather than carefully selected and justified potential confounders.
Thus, in every instance where a mediated effect was statistically significant, confounding by omitted variables remains a plausible alternative explanation for the observed associations.

Indeed, the only paper that did make a substantial effort to address confounding yielded a concerning pattern of results. Janssen et al. (2016) used a fixed-effects strategy in two timepoints of data to account for time-invariant confounders when relating monitoring to delinquency.
text.formatted: Indeed, the only paper that did make a substantial effort to address confounding yielded a concerning pattern of results. <ref type="bibr">Janssen et al. (2016)</ref> used a fixed-effects strategy in two timepoints of data to account for time-invariant confounders when relating monitoring to delinquency.

text.text: The within-person estimates of the mediated effect were 76-100% smaller than the between-person estimates of the mediated effect, and half as many were statistically significant.
This pattern suggests there may be a large amount of time-invariant confounding, which may have distorted estimates in the other papers included in this review.
Given the aforementioned methodological issues, all effect sizes should be taken with a major grain of salt.
That being said, standardized indirect effect sizes were typically small, with a median value of -0.017.
In other words, the median estimate was that a 1 SD change in monitoring would be expected to produce a 0.017 SD improvement in youth adjustment via the mediator.

While there are no widely accepted benchmarks for gauging the size of the standardized indirect effect, -0.017 is smaller than those labeled "small" in prior simulation studies (e.g., Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007).
text.formatted: While there are no widely accepted benchmarks for gauging the size of the standardized indirect effect, -0.017 is smaller than those labeled "small" in prior simulation studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The median estimate of percent mediated by the mediator was 24%.

One crude way to contextualize this effect is to notice that at 24% mediated per mediator, at least 4 completely non-overlapping mediating mechanisms would be needed to explain the full association between parental monitoring and youth adjustment.
However, estimates of percent mediated are notoriously unstable and could be calculated only for a minority of tests.
No tests of monitoring → disclosure → adjustment in longitudinal data Stattin and Kerr (2000) conceptualized youth disclosure as a competitor to parental monitoring, not a mediator.
text.formatted: No tests of monitoring → disclosure → adjustment in longitudinal data <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stattin and Kerr (2000)</ref> conceptualized youth disclosure as a competitor to parental monitoring, not a mediator.

text.text: But they did not have data that could empirically distinguish these possibilities.

It turns out that neither does the published literature: we found only one study that has tested whether disclosure mediates the association between monitoring and adjustment (Fung & Liu, 2026), and like Stattin and Kerr (2000), the authors used cross-sectional data.
text.formatted: It turns out that neither does the published literature: we found only one study that has tested whether disclosure mediates the association between monitoring and adjustment <ref type="bibr">(Fung & Liu, 2026)</ref>, and like <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stattin and Kerr (2000)</ref>, the authors used cross-sectional data.

text.text: Thus, the competitor and mediator models (Figure 1) today remain equally valid interpretations of Stattin and Kerr's classic findings.
text.formatted: Thus, the competitor and mediator models (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>) today remain equally valid interpretations of Stattin and Kerr's classic findings.

text.text: This is concerning because most scientists working on the topic assume the competitor model is correct, and it guides their design of studies and interpretation of data.
The mediator model has radically different implications not just for what Stattin and Kerr's (2000) findings actually mean, but also for how future studies should be conducted.
text.formatted: The mediator model has radically different implications not just for what <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stattin and Kerr's (2000)</ref> findings actually mean, but also for how future studies should be conducted.

text.text: Our own view is that disclosure is almost certainly both a competitor and mediator of parental monitoring.
This view would argue we need more careful measurement and methodology, and that the goal should be figuring out when and to what extent disclosure plays each role.

Such work would help not only figure out the mechanistic role of disclosure in monitoring effects, but the relative and interactive importance of monitoring and disclosure in promoting healthy adjustment.
The 13 papers that tested mediation in longitudinal data used waves spaced 6 to 60 months apart (most commonly, 12 months apart).
The absence of tests across other timescales is thus an important weakness of the evidence (Pelham et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The absence of tests across other timescales is thus an important weakness of the evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Pelham et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: No study tested mediation in monthly or weekly data, to look at mediators of shorter-term effects.
No study tested mediation in daily diary or ecological momentary assessment data to examine acute effects.
Only 1of the 39 studies included any justification for their choice of timescale (LaFreniere et al., 2022), suggesting a lack of attention to the issue rather than a careful theoretical choice.
text.formatted: Only 1of the 39 studies included any justification for their choice of timescale <ref type="bibr">(LaFreniere et al., 2022)</ref>, suggesting a lack of attention to the issue rather than a careful theoretical choice.

text.text: Nearly all tests of mediation were of the average effect of monitoring across an entire sample.
We found only 6 papers that had tested moderated mediation -mostly by teen genderand no moderated mediation finding that has been replicated in multiple samples.

The near-exclusive focus on average mediated effects is concerning because there is good reason to believe that the mechanisms by which monitoring works could differ across families and contexts (Laird et al., 2018; Pelham et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The near-exclusive focus on average mediated effects is concerning because there is good reason to believe that the mechanisms by which monitoring works could differ across families and contexts <ref type="bibr">(Laird et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Pelham et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For example, perhaps relationship quality is an important mechanism for girls but not boys, or peer affiliation is an important mechanism for older youth but not younger youth.
Such possibilities remain almost entirely uninvestigated.
Many tests in which the "mediator" is actually a measure of youth adjustment 15% of the tests (26 of 173) tested a "mediator" that was itself a measure of youth adjustment.
For example, Kiesner et al. (2010) tested whether using substances with friends mediated the association between parental monitoring and individual substance use.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Kiesner et al. (2010)</ref> tested whether using substances with friends mediated the association between parental monitoring and individual substance use.

text.text: Testing adjustment as a mediator of the effect of monitoring → adjustment has limited mechanistic value because it simply relocates the explanatory question: if monitoring affects adjustment through another form of adjustment, the mechanism linking monitoring to that intermediate form of adjustment remains unexplained.

Tests of adjustment as a mediator also had one of the highest rates of statistical significance (12 of 26 tests) among the categories of mediators -probably reflecting b paths that reflect construct continuity rather than causation per se.
The evidence did not support any firm conclusions about how mediators differ across types of parental monitoring behaviors.

Effect sizes were similar in studies that measured asking a person for information (Type 1 monitoring, or "solicitation") versus setting or enforcing rules to gather information (Type 2 monitoring, or "control").
Just 1 paper each had tested mediation of Type 3 or Type 4 monitoring.

Studies using measures that combined Types 1 and 2 monitoring yielded somewhat stronger evidence of mediation, but the choice of monitoring measure was confounded with particular outcomes and samples, rendering the difference hard to interpret.
Persistent problem of mislabeled measures Stattin and Kerr (2000) first brought attention to the issue of mislabeled measures in the study of parental monitoring.
text.formatted: Persistent problem of mislabeled measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stattin and Kerr (2000)</ref> first brought attention to the issue of mislabeled measures in the study of parental monitoring.

text.text: They clearly succeeded in raising awareness: before 2000, we could find only 1 article meeting inclusion criteria that had truly measured parental monitoring, compared to 38 articles published after 2000.
At the same time, our findings suggest the mislabeling problem has persisted.

We excluded 67 articles on the basis of a mislabeled measure of monitoring; we found many articles with "contaminated" measure of parental monitoring (e.g., 1-2 items measuring knowledge on an 8-item scale); and, since most articles do not report the full list of items on each scale, it often required contacting authors to even determine if a given paper had really measured parental monitoring.
Thus, the measurement aspect of Stattin and Kerr's critique remains incisive and relevant in 2026.
Is there any effect of monitoring → adjustment to mediate?
Stattin and Kerr (2000) were also first to question whether there is any effect of monitoring on adjustment to mediate.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stattin and Kerr (2000)</ref> were also first to question whether there is any effect of monitoring on adjustment to mediate.

text.text: The results of our review suggest there is at least an association to mediate: the median zero-order correlation between monitoring and adjustment was r = -0.13, the majority of correlations were significant (70%), and nearly all significant correlations indicated beneficial effects.
However, the same issues that reduce the rigor of the mediational analyses (e.g., exclusive use of non-experimental data) also hamper interpretation of these zero-order correlations.
Thus, the size of the total effect of monitoring is another aspect of Stattin and Kerr's critique that remains more of an open question today than one would hope.

Today, the field lacks the breadth and rigor of tests that would be needed to evaluate the mechanisms by which parental monitoring affects youth adjustment. 25 years after Stattin and Kerr first raised questions about whether and how monitoring works, we are still not in a good position to answer those questions.
We offer the following recommendations for future research in this area.
When planning a study, make sure your "monitoring" measure really measures monitoring.
When performing secondary data analysis with a suboptimal measure, be transparent about the measure's item content and qualify your interpretation of results as needed.
Given the field's fraught history, always consider listing the items on the monitoring measure verbatim in an appendix.
The goal is to figure out how monitoring affects adjustment -if the putative mediator is itself a form of adjustment, we've dodged the question rather than answered it.
Take confounding more seriously.
In non-experimental designs, consider measuring and adjusting for earlier measurements of X, M, and Y (Cole & Maxwell, 2003) as well as other potential confounders (Davis et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In non-experimental designs, consider measuring and adjusting for earlier measurements of X, M, and Y <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cole & Maxwell, 2003)</ref> as well as other potential confounders <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Davis et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Collecting ≥3 waves of data to establish temporal precedence would help, as would performing sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding (Liu et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Collecting ≥3 waves of data to establish temporal precedence would help, as would performing sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Liu et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Consider also experimental designs in which parental monitoring and/or the putative mediator are manipulated - Valente et al. (2017) and Bullock et al. (2010) describe some options.
text.formatted: Consider also experimental designs in which parental monitoring and/or the putative mediator are manipulated - <ref type="bibr">Valente et al. (2017)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bullock et al. (2010)</ref> describe some options.

text.text: Recognize that mechanisms may differ across monitoring behaviors, outcomes, timescales, families, or contexts.
Avoid one-size-fits-all thinking and prematurely generalizing early findings.
As more tests accumulate, finer testing for differences will become possible and may reveal the mechanisms by which monitoring affects adjustment vary along several characteristics.
Only 10% of papers reported the coefficient and standard error for every estimate of a, b, and c' -this proved a big obstacle to meta-analysis.
Standardized effect sizes were reported in only 26% of papers.
As the field performs more tests, authors could follow a mediation reporting checklist (e.g., Lee et al., 2021) to ensure the accumulated evidence will be amenable to meta-analytic synthesis.
text.formatted: As the field performs more tests, authors could follow a mediation reporting checklist (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lee et al., 2021)</ref> to ensure the accumulated evidence will be amenable to meta-analytic synthesis.

text.text: We have already discussed several important limitations of the underlying literature (e.g., cross-sectional samples, lack of attention to confounding) and how they seriously qualify the interpretation of results.
We close with two important limitations of our review.
The first is that we only reviewed studies that tested a statistical mediation model.
Thus, we may be missing mechanistic evidence coming from other designs (e.g., experiments, qualitative interviews) or from studies that estimated just a, or just b and c'.
The second limitation is that we focused narrowly on mediators of a single, unidirectional path: that from parental monitoring to youth adjustment.

The broader parent-youth monitoring process involves many other links of interest (Pelham et al., 2024) and this study could not evaluate the extent to which the mechanistic evidence for monitoring→adjustment is stronger or weaker than for the links between other constructs.

text.text: A major goal for the next 25 years after Stattin and Kerr will be to gain a deeper mechanistic understanding of how the various pieces of the information management puzzle fit together.

Evidence base describes the number of papers and number of tests found within a particular grouping.

Pattern of significance relays the number of statistically significant tests within a grouping and how many of those significant tests were beneficial (leading to better youth adjustment outcomes) or detrimental (leading to worse youth adjustment outcomes).
Standardized mediated effect provides mean, median, and range for all indirect effects that are standardized within a given grouping.
Percent mediated provides mean, median, and range of the percent the indirect effects mediated the total effects for all applicable tests in a given grouping.
Interquartile range (IQR) is provided as well for the "Overall" grouping for both "Standardized mediated effect" and "Percent mediated."
We reported percent mediated if we could find it in the paper or if it could be calculated (indirect effect is available, direct effect is available, and signs of direct and indirect effects match).
Table excludes tests of sequential mediation or moderated mediation.

text.text: The supplementary material includes a file tabulated-data.xlsx that includes all the data extracted from the included articles and tabulated for this review.
The spreadsheet has two tabs: • The second tab is called "data" and has all the extracted data.
There is 1 row per estimate of mediation (k = 223).
• The first tab is called "metadata" and says what each column in the "data" tab means.
For example, this sheet tells you that the column "sample_nobs" in the "data" tab reports "the total N for the test given by the article."
• A cell in the "data" tab that has the phrase "[not reported]" in it is indicating that the given value was not reported in the paper.

A cell with the phrase "[not applicable]" in it is indicating that the given value is not applicable for the given test / row because there is no value to provide to begin with (e.g., m2_authorlabel would be "[not applicable]" if there was only one mediator in the test)
If the paper reported the standardized indirect effect (ab) or the percent of the total effect that was mediated by the indirect effect, we used the reported number.
If the paper did not report these effect sizes, we tried to calculate them where possible.
If the indirect effect was not reported, but a standardized a and standardized b were reported, we would calculate standardized ab by multiplying the a path and the b path:
We only did this calculation when the M regression and Y regression were linear.

If the reported or calculated indirect effect was not already standardized, we would calculate the standardized ab by multiplying ab with the the standard deviation of X divided by the standard deviation of Y:
We only did this calculation when the M regression and Y regression were linear.
